'''Waddesdon Manor''' is a [[English country house|country house]] in the village of [[Waddesdon]], in [[Buckinghamshire]], England. Owned by the [[National Trust]] and managed by the Rothschild Foundation, it is one of the National Trust's most visited properties, with over 463,000 visitors in 2019.<ref name="ALVA 2019 visitor numbers">{{cite web |title=ALVA - Association of Leading Visitor Attractions |url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |website=www.alva.org.uk |access-date=23 October 2020}}</ref>

The Grade I listed house was built in a mostly [[Neo-Renaissance]] style, copying individual features of several French [[château]]x, between 1874 and 1889 for Baron [[Ferdinand de Rothschild]] (1839–1898) as a weekend residence for entertaining and to house his collection of arts and antiquities. As the manor and estate have passed through three generations of the [[Rothschild family]], the contents of the house have expanded to become one of the most rare and valuable collections in the world.<ref>{{cite web|title=History's riches: Inside the private collection of a Rothschild heir|url=https://edition.cnn.com/style/article/rothschild-collection/index.html|website=www.cnn.com|date=4 October 2019|author=Matthew Ponsford|access-date=25 August 2020}}</ref> In 1957, [[James de Rothschild (politician)|James de Rothschild]] bequeathed the house and its contents to the National Trust, opening the house and gardens for the benefit of the general public. Unusually for a National Trust property, the family of James Rothschild, the donor, manage the house. The Rothschild Foundation, chaired by Dame [[Hannah Rothschild (film maker)|Hannah Rothschild]], continues to invest in the property.<ref>{{cite web|title=Inside Lord Jacob Rothschild's Monolithic English Country Estate|url=https://www.vogue.com/article/lord-jacob-rothschild-english-estate|website=www.vogue.com|date=29 January 2016|author=Jane Withers|access-date=25 August 2020}}</ref>

==History==
===1874–1898===
[[File:Aerial view of Waddesdon Manor from the north.jpg|left|alt= Aerial view of Waddesdon from the north|thumb|upright=1.5|Aerial view of Waddesdon from the north]]
[[File:Red Drawing Room at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|250px|thumb|The Red Drawing Room]]
There had been a medieval [[manor house]], probably moated, on the estate, now vanished.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Waddesdon - Buckinghamshire's Heritage Portal |url=https://heritageportal.buckinghamshire.gov.uk/theme/tbc762 |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20250502200209/https://heritageportal.buckinghamshire.gov.uk/theme/tbc762 |archive-date=2025-05-02 |access-date=2025-12-22 |website=heritageportal.buckinghamshire.gov.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref> In 1874, [[Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild]] bought the Waddesdon agricultural estate from [[John Spencer-Churchill, 7th Duke of Marlborough]] with money inherited from his father [[Anselm Salomon von Rothschild|Anselm]]. Rothschild was familiar with the estate from fox hunting in the locality. At the time of purchase, the estate had no house, park or garden. The site of the future manor house was a bare hill known as Lodge Hill, which had been stripped of its timber by the impoverished Duke of Marlborough prior to the sale.<ref>Hall, pp. 37–41</ref> Over the following three years, the summit of the hill was levelled; eventually, on 18 August 1877, the foundation stone was laid.

The first house party was held in May 1880 with seven of Rothschild's close male friends enjoying a [[fireworks]] display. When, finally, the main house was ready in 1883, Rothschild invited 20 guests to stay. Before his premature death in 1898, on weekends between May and September, [[Baron]] de Rothschild was host to many important guests, including Albert Edward, [[Prince of Wales]] (the future King [[Edward VII]]). House parties usually involved 14 to 20 guests.<ref>[https://family.rothschildarchive.org/estates/48-waddesdon-manor The Rothschild Archive] Retrieved 28 September 2015; Hall, pp. 153,162</ref>

Guests commented on the level of luxury service provided by the 24 house staff.<ref>Hall, pp. 156, 160</ref> In 1890, [[Queen Victoria]] unusually requested to pay a visit. She was impressed with the beauty of the house and grounds as well as Rothschild's ability to quietly manage the day's events. She was struck by the newly installed electric lights designed to look like candles in the chandeliers, and it is reported that she asked for the room to be darkened to fully witness the effect.<ref>Hall, p. 172</ref>

===1898–1957===
[[File:WMGIanoGPEG.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Plan of Waddesdon's ground floor. 1:Vestibule; 2:Entrance Hall, 3 Red Drawing room; 4:Grey Drawing Room; 5:Library; 6:Baron's Sitting room; 7:Morning Room; 8:West Hall; 9:West Gallery; 10:East Gallery; 11:Dining Room; 12:Conservatory; 13:Breakfast Room; 14:Kitchen; 15:Servant's Hall; 16:Housekeeper's Rooms; 17:Site of further servants quarters (not illustrated); 18:Terrace and parterre; 19 North Drive; St:staircases.]]
When Baron Ferdinand died in 1898, the house passed to his sister [[Alice Charlotte von Rothschild|Alice de Rothschild]]. She saw Waddesdon as a memorial for her brother and was committed to preserving it. She did add significant items to the collection, particularly furniture and carpets with French royal provenances, [[Meissen porcelain]], textiles and [[armour]].<ref>Hall, pp. 180–91</ref>
[[File:Entryway - Waddesdon Manor - Buckinghamshire, England - DSC07600.jpg|thumb|Front entrance]]
Following Alice de Rothschild's death in 1922, the property and collections passed to her French great-nephew [[James de Rothschild (politician)|James de Rothschild]], who was married to an English woman, [[Dorothy de Rothschild|Dorothy Pinto]]. James further enriched the manor with objects from the collections of his late father Baron [[Edmond James de Rothschild]] of Paris.<ref>Girouard, p. 55</ref>

James and Dorothy hosted a [[Liberal Party (UK)|Liberal Party]] rally at Waddesdon in 1928, where [[David Lloyd George]] addressed the crowd.<ref>''Selection of pamphlets & leaflets'', (Liberal Publication Dept., 1928), p. 213; see also [http://collection.waddesdon.org.uk/search.do?id=41323&db=object&page=1&view=detail Waddesdon Manor, acc. no. 894], Retrieved 11 January 2016</ref> During World War II, children under the age of five were evacuated from [[Croydon]] and lived at Waddesdon Manor, the only time children lived in the house. James and Dorothy also provided asylum at Waddesdon for a group of Jewish boys from Frankfurt.<ref>[http://www.migrationmuseum.org/100imagesgallery/cedar-boys/ ''The Cedar Boys, Waddesdon Manor, 1944''] Retrieved 17 May 2017</ref>

===1957–1997===
When James de Rothschild died in 1957, he bequeathed Waddesdon Manor, {{convert|120|acre|ha}} of grounds and its contents to the [[National Trust]], to be preserved for posterity. Dorothy moved to nearby [[Eythrope]] and the manor was never again used as a residence. It opened to the public in 1959, with around 27,000 visitors in the first year.<ref>Hall, p. 268</ref> Dorothy chaired the new management committee in close collaboration with the National Trust and took a very keen interest in Waddesdon for the remainder of her long life.<ref>Rothschild, 1979</ref>
[[File:Morning Room at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|thumb|right|Dutch and English paintings in the Morning Room]]
At Dorothy's death, in 1989, her nephew [[Jacob Rothschild, 4th Baron Rothschild|Jacob Rothschild]] inherited her position and responsibilities. In March 1990, Jacob succeeded his father to become the fourth [[Baron Rothschild]]. At Lord Rothschild's initiative, the manor underwent a major restoration from 1990 to 1997, and the visitor attractions were enhanced, including the creation of the Waddesdon Wine Cellars.

===1997–2019===
Until his death in February 2024, [[Jacob Rothschild, 4th Baron Rothschild|Lord Rothschild]] chaired the family charity handling Waddesdon's management, the Rothschild Foundation.<ref>[http://www.rothschildfoundation.org.uk/areas-of-interest/waddesdon-manor/ The Rothschild Foundation] Retrieved 29 September 2015; {{EW charity|1138145|THE ROTHSCHILD FOUNDATION}} previously {{EW charity|290859|"The Alice Trust"}} Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> Waddesdon Manor operates as an independent organisation within the National Trust.

From 2004 to 2006, the Baron's Room and Green Boudoir were restored to reflect Baron Ferdinand's original arrangements.<ref>Hall, p. 299</ref> In 2003 a burglary was committed involving [[the Johnson Gang]], when approximately 100 gold snuff boxes and other items were stolen from the collection prompting the installation of new security measures.<ref>[https://waddesdon.org.uk/about-us/governance/gold-box-theft/ Gold box theft of 2003], Waddesdon Manor website; [https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2006/oct/11/arts.ukcrime "Police arrest gang"], ''[[The Guardian]]'', Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> In 2021 one small sweet-box from this theft was identified at auction and returned to Waddesdon.<ref name="Sherwood2022">{{cite news |last1=Sherwood |first1=Harriet |title=Gold box stolen in 2003 Waddesdon Manor heist is returned home |url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2022/apr/24/gold-box-stolen-in-2003-waddesdon-manor-heist-is-returned-home |access-date=24 April 2022 |work=The Guardian |issue=24 April 2022}}</ref>

Since 2004, there has been an exhibitions programme. Notable exhibitions include the [[Lod Mosaic Archaeological Center|Lod Mosaic]] in 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.spectator.co.uk/spectator-life/spectator-life-culture/9232521/full-house/ |title=Lord Rothschild interview |date=21 June 2014 |work=[[The Spectator]] |author=Cristina Odone}} Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> Waddesdon was one venue celebrating the work of [[Henry Moore]] in 2015<ref>[http://www.countrylife.co.uk/art-and-antiques/exhibition-review-henry-moore-ysp-waddesdon-leeds-art-gallery-73994 Exhibition review: Henry Moore at YSP, Waddesdon and Leeds Art Gallery] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304193031/http://www.countrylife.co.uk/art-and-antiques/exhibition-review-henry-moore-ysp-waddesdon-leeds-art-gallery-73994 |date=4 March 2016 }} Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> and [[Eliot Hodgkin]] in 2019.<ref>[https://www.countrylife.co.uk/publication/country-life/country-life-17-june-2019 Exhibition review of Brought to Life: Eliot Hodgkin Rediscovered] Retrieved 7 August 2019</ref>

New works of art have been acquired by the Rothschild Foundation to complement the existing collections at Waddesdon, such as ''Le Faiseur de Châteaux de Cartes'' by [[Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin]], added in 2007.

There has also been a programme of engagement with contemporary artists, beginning with [[Angus Fairhurst]] represented by [[Arnolfini, Bristol|Arnolfini]] in 2009. Works have been sited near the Manor and on the wider estate including by [[Richard Long (artist)|Richard Long]], [[Sarah Lucas]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ft.com/intl/cms/s/2/47201662-99fd-11e1-aa6d-00144feabdc0.html?ftcamp=published_links%2Frss%2Fmagazine%2Ffeed%2F%2Fproduct&ftcamp=crm/email/2012512/nbe/ArtsLeisure/product#axzz1ug4WjVs8 |title=Art, chez Rothschild |date=12 May 2012 |work=[[Financial Times]] |author=Rachel Spence}}Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> In 2012, [[Christie's]] chose the manor to exhibit sculptures by leading contemporary artists.<ref>[http://www.christies.com/about/press-center/releases/pressrelease.aspx?pressreleaseid=5615 Christie's at Waddesdon Manor] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304233005/http://www.christies.com/about/press-center/releases/pressrelease.aspx?pressreleaseid=5615 |date=4 March 2016 }} Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref>

Between 2013 and 2017, [[Bruce Munro]] had a residency at Waddesdon Manor, beginning with the music and light piece ''Cantus Arcticus'' in the Coach House Gallery in 2013. ''Winter Light'' (2013), with its distinctive wigwam-type structures sited in the gardens of the manor, was Munro's first solo exhibition of his large-scale pieces; ''Winter Light'' returned in 2016–2017. In 2014, Munro developed his pod-like structures, adding elements of language in ''Snow Code'', shown in the manor. In ''...---...SOS'', Munro's winter exhibition of 2015–2016, tents were lit up in tune with sound, in response to images of [[Emergency management|disaster relief]].<ref>[http://www.craftscouncil.org.uk/articles/winter-light/ Winter Light] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180712023317/http://www.craftscouncil.org.uk/articles/winter-light/ |date=12 July 2018 }} Retrieved 28 September 2015; [http://www.brucemunro.co.uk/exhibitions/ List of exhibitions by Bruce Munro] Retrieved 18 May 2017</ref>
[[File:Jan Baptist Xavery - Flora.jpg|thumb|170px|''Flora'' by [[Jan Baptist Xavery]], bedroom corridor]]
In 2012, [[Edmund de Waal]] exhibited work in the manor, creating a dialogue between his work and the historical interiors.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2012/apr/20/edmund-de-waal-amber-eyes |title=Edmund de Waal turns Amber Eyes towards Waddesdon |date=20 April 2012 |work=[[The Guardian]] |author=Mark Brown}} Retrieved 26 April 2017</ref> In 2015, artist [[Joana Vasconcelos]] was commissioned to install two sculptures entitled ''Lafite'' in front of the Manor.<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SF8spZ0SA7E Joana Vasconcelos in conversation with Jacob Rothschild about the Lafite sculpture at Waddesdon] Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> In 2016, [[Kate Malone]] exhibited a collection of new work inspired by the people, gardens, collections, and archive.<ref>'From the Manor drawn', [https://www.ceramicreview.com/magazine/ "Ceramic Review"], July/Aug 2016</ref> Two [[portrait]] pots of Baron Ferdinand and [[Alice Charlotte von Rothschild|Alice de Rothschild]] by Malone remain on display at the Manor.<ref>[https://waddesdon.org.uk/kate-malone-inspired-waddesdon/ Kate Malone: Inspired by Waddesdon] Retrieved 18 May 2017</ref>

==Architecture==
Prior to the construction of Waddesdon Manor, no house existed on the site. Ferdinand de Rothschild wanted a house in the style of the great Renaissance [[châteaux of the Loire Valley]].<ref>Girouard, p. 22</ref> Ferdinand chose as his architect [[Gabriel-Hippolyte Destailleur]].<ref>Girouard, p. 23</ref> Destailleur was already experienced in working in this style, having overseen the restoration of many châteaux in that region, in particular that of the Château de Mouchy.
[[File:Waddesden Manor03.JPG|thumb|upright=1.4|left|The terrace and [[parterre]] garden at Waddesdon Manor, overlooked by the building's south facade]]
Through Destailleur's vision, Waddesdon embodied an [[Eclecticism|eclectic]] style based on the châteaux so admired by his patron, Baron Ferdinand. The towers at Waddesdon were based on those of the [[Château de Maintenon]], and the twin [[staircase tower]]s, on the north façade, were inspired by the staircase tower at the [[Château de Chambord]].<ref>Girouard, p. 24</ref> However, following the theme of unparalleled luxury at Waddesdon, the windows of the towers at Waddesdon were glazed, unlike those of the staircase at Chambord. They are also far more ornate.

The structural design of Waddesdon was not entirely retrospective. Hidden from view were the most modern innovations of the late 19th century including a steel frame, which took the strain of walls on the upper floors, and which consequently permitted the layout of these floors to differ completely from the lower floors.<ref name="Girouard, p. 34">Girouard, p. 34</ref> The house also had hot and cold running water in its bathrooms, central heating, and an electric bell system to summon the numerous servants. The building contractor was Edward Conder & Son.<ref name="Girouard, p. 34"/>

After the manor was completed in 1883, Ferdinand quickly decided it was too small, as his architect had prophesied. The Bachelors' Wing to the east was extended after 1885 and the Morning Room, built in late-[[Gothic style]], was added to the west after 1888.<ref>Bruno Pons, ''Waddesdon Manor Architecture and Panelling: The James A. de Rothschild Bequest at Waddesdon Manor'' (London, 1996), pp. 77–95</ref> The stables to the west of the manor were built in 1884. Ferdinand and his stud groom devised the plan, working with Conder. Destailleur designed the facades in a French 17th-century style.<ref>Hall, p. 66</ref>
{{clear}}

===Wine cellars===
[[File:The wine cellars at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|The wine cellars]]
The wine cellars in the manor were created during the centenary restoration and opened in 1994. They are modelled on the private cellars at [[Château Lafite Rothschild]]. More than 15,000 bottles are stored in the Cellars, some 150 years old, the majority from the [[Château Lafite Rothschild]] and [[Château Mouton Rothschild]] estates. It is the largest private collection of Rothschild wines in the world. There are also wine labels designed by artists such as [[Salvador Dalí]] and [[Andy Warhol]].<ref>Schwartz, pp. 118–120</ref>

==Collections==
[[File:Pedestal clock by André-Charles Boulle, movement by George Graham, 1720-1725 - Waddesdon Manor - Buckinghamshire, England - DSC07655.jpg|thumb|right|180px|Pedestal clock attributed to [[André-Charles Boulle]], movement by [[George Graham (clockmaker)|George Graham]], 1720–1725]]
Once his château was complete, Baron Ferdinand installed his extensive collections of English 18th-century portraits by artists like [[Thomas Gainsborough|Gainsborough]] and [[Joshua Reynolds|Reynolds]], as well as French 18th-century [[boiseries]], [[Savonnerie manufactory|Savonnerie]] carpets, [[Gobelins manufactory|Gobelins]] and [[Beauvais tapestry|Beauvais]] tapestries, furniture, [[Manufacture nationale de Sèvres|Sèvres]] ceramics, books, Dutch paintings and [[Renaissance]] treasures.
[[File:East Gallery at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|thumb|left|The Elephant Automaton in the East Gallery]]
Works were acquired for their exquisite quality and fine provenance, particularly those belonging to French royalty of the [[Ancien Régime]]. One of the highlights of the collection is the extraordinary musical [[automaton]] elephant, dating from 1774 and made by the French [[clockmaker]] H Martinet.<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7YEPhe2Gp0Y A Marvellous Elephant] Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref>
[[File:Grey Drawing Room at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|thumb|right|Grey Drawing Room with fine 18th-century French panelling and a [[Manufacture nationale de Sèvres|Sèvres]] ship-vase in situ]]
Of the ten surviving examples of the [[Sèvres pot-pourri vase in the shape of a ship]] from the 1760s, three are at Waddesdon, including one with a very rare scene of a battle connected to the [[Seven Years' War]].<ref>[http://collection.waddesdon.org.uk/search.do?view=detail&page=1&id=41419&db=object Pot-pourri vase, 1761, Waddesdon Manor, acc. no. 2315] Retrieved 11 January 2016</ref>
[[File:Smoking Room at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|thumb|left|The restored Smoking Room with Renaissance treasures]]
In the 1890s, Baron Ferdinand focused on the Renaissance collection for his small museum in the New Smoking Room.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.apollo-magazine.com/in-praise-of-the-waddesdon-bequest/ |title=In praise of the Waddesdon Bequest |date=15 May 2015 |work=[[Apollo (magazine)|Apollo]] |author=Katy Barrett}} Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref> This collection was bequeathed to the [[British Museum]] and is now known as the [[Waddesdon Bequest]].<ref>[https://www.britishmuseum.org/explore/galleries/themes/room_2a_waddesdon_bequest.aspx The Waddesdon Bequest A Rothschild Renaissance] Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref>

The interior of Waddesdon Manor was photographed in 1897 for Baron Ferdinand's privately published ''The Red Book''.<ref>[https://waddesdon.org.uk/blog/the-red-book/ Waddesdon Manor blog entry, with link to the whole book online.]</ref>

Subsequent members of the family added noted collections of paintings, [[Limoges enamel]], arms and armour, [[maiolica]], manuscripts, prints and drawings.

Waddesdon's internationally famous collection has thus been formed principally by four members of the Rothschild family: Baron Ferdinand (1839–1898), his sister [[Alice Charlotte von Rothschild|Alice de Rothschild]] (1847–1922), their cousin [[Edmond James de Rothschild]] (1845–1934) and [[Jacob Rothschild, 4th Baron Rothschild]] (1936–2024).<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6tmG7sUmZwM Art Collections at Waddesdon Manor] Retrieved 21 June 2016</ref>

==Gardens==
Baron Ferdinand wanted a garden to entertain his guests during his weekend house parties. To make the gardens, extensive [[Landscape architecture|landscaping]] of the hill was carried out, including leveling the top of the hill. The gardens and landscape park were laid out by the French landscape architect [[Elie Lainé]]. An attempt was made to transplant full-grown trees by [[chloroform]]ing their roots, to limit the shock. While this novel idea was unsuccessful, many very large trees were successfully transplanted. Elaborate flower beds were planted, centred on the south Parterre. Several artificial rock formations were created by [[James Pulham and Son|James Pulham]], including to house mountain goats and llamas, part of [[Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild|Ferdinand's]] zoo.<ref>Hall, pp. 64–66, 127</ref> Altogether, the creation of his garden cost £153,000, which (in terms of average wages then and in 2015) equates to £68.8 million.<ref>Floud, Roderick, ''An Economic History of the English Garden'', p. 12, 2019, Allen Lane, {{isbn|9780241235577}}</ref>
[[File:Bird - Waddesdon Manor - Buckinghamshire, England - DSC07580.jpg|alt=3D bird|thumb|Three-dimensional bedding in the shape of a bird]]
After her brother's death [[Alice Charlotte von Rothschild|Alice]] brought the care she had taken with her garden at [[Eythrope]] to Waddesdon. Alice was a keen gardener with a good understanding of flowers and plants; she would often walk around and weed the paths. With her head gardener, George Frederick Johnson who worked at Waddesdon from 1905 to 1954, Alice grew flowers for competition.<ref>Hall, pp. 194–206</ref> Alice was responsible for introducing three-dimensional bedding in the shape of a bird, recreated in the gardens today.<ref>Schwartz, p. 127</ref>

Under [[James de Rothschild (politician)|James]], the gardens were less impressive. The South Parterre was grassed over in the 1930s. It was replanted with flowers for the opening of the house under the National Trust in 1959.<ref>Hall, pp. 267–68</ref>

As part of the 1990s restoration, Beth Rothschild led a team reintroducing Ferdinand's colour scheme of trees, shrubs and [[bedding plant]]s. The [[carpet bedding]] is now designed on computer allowing the schemes to be quickly installed. The patterns change each year to reflect different themes.<ref>Hall, pp. 286–91</ref>

The gardens are listed Grade I on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1000446|desc=Waddesdon Manor|access-date=9 February 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>

===Garden trees===
Though the trees are not of a great age there are many specimens of [[deciduous]] and [[coniferous]] trees that have now reached maturity creating the desired effect in the Waddesdon [[landscape]]. Some of these trees were planted in the 1870s and responsibility for this fell to William Barron whose job it was to transplant trees from the surrounding countryside to give the grounds of Waddesdon a sense of maturity, creating vistas and focal points under the instructions from [[Elie Lainé]].<ref>Graham Stuart Thomas, ''Great gardens of Britain'', (Mayflower: 1979), p. 236</ref>

Deciduous trees were selected on their form, flowering and array of autumnal colour. Conifers were selected for their evergreen nature, cones and berries. Today many species such as [[chestnut]]s, [[Tilia|limes]] and [[maple]]s as well as [[yew]], [[Cedrus|cedar]]s and [[Sequoioideae|redwoods]] can be seen.

From Baron Ferdinand's time to today, distinguished visitors have been invited to plant memorial trees. [[Queen Victoria]], King [[Edward VII]], King [[George V]] and [[Mary of Teck|Queen Mary]] were early royal visitors.<ref>D. de Rothschild, pp. 54–55</ref> [[Charles III]] (as Prince of Wales) and Prime Ministers Sir [[John Major]] and [[Tony Blair]] have also planted trees.{{citation needed|date=July 2025}}

===Garden sculptures===
Baron Ferdinand acquired many fine [[statue]]s and [[fountain]]s to add interest to the gardens. A notable feature is his love of 18th-century Italian pieces. The fountains to the north and south of the house include sculptures of [[Pluto (mythology)|Pluto]], [[Proserpina]], [[Triton (mythology)|triton]]s and [[nereid]]s originally made by Giuliano Mozani around 1720 for the [[Ducal Palace of Colorno]].<ref>T. Hodgkinson, ''Sculpture: The James A de Rothschild Collection at Waddesdon Manor'' (1970)</ref> A bust of the [[muse]] [[Erato]] has been recently attributed to [[Filippo Parodi]].<ref>Maichol Clemente, 'Un busto di Filippo Parodi a Waddesdon Manor', ''Arte Veneta'', 68 (2012), pp. 258–259</ref>

A fine example of French early 18th-century [[sculpture]] is sited near the Aviary: [[Apollo]] by Jean Raon, 1699, associated with a commission at [[Palace of Versailles|Versailles]]. There are also Dutch vases in the style of [[Albert Jansz Vinckenbrinck]] and sculptures by [[Jan van Logteren]], the latter were originally displayed at [[Aston Clinton House]].<ref>Michael Hall, 'An acquisitive gene: Lord Rothschild's collecting for Waddesdon', "Apollo" (July-Aug 2007), pp. 44–49</ref>

In 2001, [[Stephen Cox (sculptor)|Stephen Cox]]'s tomb-like sculpture ''Interior Space: Terra degli Etruschi'' was installed at the end of the Baron's Walk. Inscribed on a nearby marble slab are the names of the Rothschilds who built and have cared for Waddesdon.

===Aviary===
[[File:Aviary at Waddesdon Manor.jpg|alt=Waddesdon Manor aviary|thumb|Waddesdon Manor aviary]]
Baron Ferdinand also created a cast-iron [[aviary]], inspired by 18th-century [[pavilion]]s at the [[Palace of Versailles]] and [[Château de Chantilly]], as well as his childhood home at Grüneburg. It was completed in 1889. Like other members of his family, such as [[Walter Rothschild, 2nd Baron Rothschild]], Ferdinand was also a keen animal lover. He stocked the aviary with exotic birds and enjoyed feeding them for his guests.<ref>Hall, pp. 66, 125</ref>

The aviary's paint and gilding were restored in 2003 and it now houses endangered species with a focus on breeding programs. It is a registered [[zoo]].<ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=prsXzDCRh-w The Aviary at Waddesdon Manor] Retrieved 20 June 2016</ref>

==Estate==
In Ferdinand's time, there was a large kitchen garden and extensive [[Greenhouse|glass houses]] growing fruit and flowers, including Ferdinand's beloved [[orchid]]s. They were near the Dairy [[Water garden]] which has elaborate rock formations by [[James Pulham and Son|James Pulham]]. As part of the day's entertainments, Ferdinand's guests were taken to the ornamental Dairy to taste milk from cows who wore [[Meissen porcelain]] name tags.<ref>Schwartz, pp. 132–133</ref>

In recent years, commissions to contemporary architects have occurred on the wider estate. [[Windmill Hill, Buckinghamshire|Windmill Hill Archive]] (2011) was designed by Stephen Marshall.<ref>{{cite web|title=Whistle down the windmill|work=World Architecture News|url=http://www.worldarchitecturenews.com/project/2011/16869/stephen-marshall-architects-llp/waddesdon-manor-windmill-hill-in-aylesbury.html|access-date=29 September 2015}}</ref> [[Flint House, Buckinghamshire|Flint House]] (2015) was designed by [[Charlotte Skene-Catling]] of Skene Catling de la Peña.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Wainwright|first1=Oliver|title=Flint House|url=https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/architecture-design-blog/2015/jul/10/flint-house-waddesdon-manor-rothschild-skene-catling-de-la-pena|website=The Guardian|date=10 July 2015 |access-date=29 September 2015}}</ref> It won RIBA House of the Year in 2015.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.architecture.com/StirlingPrize/Awards2015/House%20of%20the%20Year/RIBAHouseoftheYear2015.aspx |title=Flint House wins|date=25 November 2015 |publisher=[[Royal Institute of British Architects]]}} Retrieved 4 January 2016</ref>

In 2012, it was announced that Waddesdon Manor would be one of the sites for Jubilee Woodlands, designated by the [[Woodland Trust]] to commemorate [[Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee]].<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-beds-bucks-herts-16532190 Queen's Jubilee wood at Waddeson Manor needs volunteers] Retrieved 28 September 2015</ref>

==Film and television==
Many films have been shot at Waddesdon Manor, including the ''[[Carry On (franchise)|Carry On]]'' film ''[[Don't Lose Your Head]]'' (1966); ''[[Never Say Never Again]]'' (1983); ''[[An Ideal Husband (1999 film)|An Ideal Husband]]'' (1999); {{Lang|hi-latn|[[Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham]]}} (2001), ''[[Ladies in Lavender]]'' (2004); ''[[Ripley Under Ground]]'' (2005); ''[[The Queen (2006 film)|The Queen]]'' (2006); ''[[The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor]]'' (2008); ''[[Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows]]'' (2011); ''[[A Little Chaos]]'' (2014); ''[[Victor Frankenstein (film)|Victor Frankenstein]]'' (2015), ''[[Our Kind of Traitor (film)|Our Kind of Traitor]]'' (2016); ''[[The Infiltrator (2016 film)|The Infiltrator]]'' (2016); [[Cinderella (2021 American film)|''Cinderella'']] (2021); and ''[[Back in Action (2025 film)|Back In Action]]'' (2025).<ref name="imdb-2016">{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/search/title?locations=Waddesdon%20Manor,%20Waddesdon,%20Buckinghamshire,%20England,%20UK|title=IMDb, Waddesdon Manor Location|website=[[IMDb]] |access-date=15 May 2017}}</ref>

Waddesdon Manor has also been used as a location for a number of television programmes. These include ''[[Howards' Way]]'' (1985), ''[[Downton Abbey]]'' (2011), ''[[And Then There Were None (miniseries)|And Then There Were None]]'' ([[BBC One]], 2015), ''[[The Crown (TV series)|The Crown]]'' (2016),<ref name="imdb-2016" /> ''[[Endeavour (TV series)|Endeavour]]'' and ''[[Queen Charlotte: A Bridgerton Story]]'' (2023).<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/search/title/?at=0&locations=Waddesdon%20Manor,%20Waddesdon,%20Buckinghamshire,%20England,%20UK&sort=year,desc IMDb list]</ref>

{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2019}}

'''Anglesey Abbey''' is a [[National Trust]] property in the village of [[Lode, Cambridgeshire|Lode]], {{convert|5+1/2|mi|km}} northeast of [[Cambridge]], [[England]]. The property includes a [[English country house|country house]], built on the remains of a [[priory]], 98 acres (400,000 m<sup>2</sup>) of gardens and landscaped grounds, and a working mill.
 
The priory was closed in 1536 during the [[dissolution of the monasteries]] and a [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean-style]] house was built on the site of the ruins in about 1600. Owners down the centuries included [[Thomas Hobson (postal carrier)|Thomas Hobson]] and his Parker descendants, and three local clergymen. The last private owner was [[Urban Huttleston Broughton, 1st Baron Fairhaven|Lord Fairhaven]] who lived in the house from 1926 until he died in 1966. He made extensive additions to the house to accommodate his collection of furniture, art, books and objets d'art and landscaped the grounds. On his death, he left the house and its contents to the National Trust.

==History==

Anglesey Abbey was built on the remains of a priory of Augustinian [[Canons regular]], which was founded as a hospital of [[St Mary]] during the reign of [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] (i.e., between 1100 and 1135) and endowed as a priory by [[Richard de Clare, 3rd Earl of Hertford|Richard de Clare]] in 1212. The priory was closed in 1536 during the [[dissolution of the monasteries]]. Three years later it was granted to a lawyer, [[John Hynde]].<ref>{{cite book |chapter=Houses of Augustinian canons: Priory of Anglesey |title=A History of the County of Cambridge and the Isle of Ely: Volume 2 |editor-first=L. F. |editor-last=Salzman |location=London |date=1948 |pages=229–234 |via=British History Online |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/cambs/vol2/pp229-234 |accessdate=28 February 2020}}</ref> The priory was largely demolished and materials used in the construction of [[Madingley Hall]].<ref>{{cite book |chapter=Madingley |title=An Inventory of the Historical Monuments in the County of Cambridgeshire, Volume 1, West Cambridgeshire |location=London |date=1968 |pages=176–188 |via=British History Online |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/rchme/cambs/vol1/pp176-188 |accessdate=28 February 2020}}</ref>

[[File:Anglesey Abbey 3a.jpg|left|thumb|upright=1.4|Visitor entrance at rear of house, with dining room on the right showing old masonry]]

The Fowkes family acquired the property in 1595 and converted what remained of the demolished priory into a [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean-style]] house.<ref name="NHLE">{{NHLE|num=1000611|desc=Anglesey Abbey, Lode |accessdate=29 February 2020}}</ref> The walls of the [[chapter house]] were incorporated into the main part of the domestic dwelling, with the [[calefactory]] or monks' day room to the north left as an outbuilding.<ref name="Guide">{{cite book | last1 = Fedden | first1 = Robin| title = Anglesey Abbey: A Guide | date = 1980 | publisher = National Trust}}</ref>{{rp|6–7}} Subsequent owners included the Cambridge carrier [[Thomas Hobson (postal carrier)|Thomas Hobson]] (of "Hobson's Choice"), his son-in-law barrister Thomas Parker and descendants, Cambridgeshire MP [[Samuel Shepheard (died 1748)|Samuel Shepheard]] and his daughter Lady Irvine, and [[George Leonard Jenyns]]. Owners did not always occupy the house themselves; it was leased out as a farmhouse at times.<ref name="Bottisham">{{cite book |first1=A. F. |last1=Wareham |first2=A. P. M. |last2=Wright |chapter=Bottisham: Manors and other estates |title=A History of the County of Cambridge and the Isle of Ely: Volume 10, Cheveley, Flendish, Staine and Staploe Hundreds (North-Eastern Cambridgeshire) |location=London |date=2002 |pages=196–205 |via=British History Online |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/cambs/vol10/pp196-205 |accessdate=2 March 2020}}.</ref> By the time Thomas Parker died in 1643 the property was known as Anglesey Abbey, rather than Priory.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/D864341 |title=Catalogue description of Will of Thomas Parker of Anglesey Abbey |website=National Archives |access-date=28 February 2020}}</ref>

In 1848 Reverend John Hailstone, vicar of the neighbouring parish of [[Bottisham]], son of botanist [[Samuel Hailstone]] and nephew of a geologist [[John Hailstone]], purchased Anglesey Abbey and carried out restorations, converting the monks' day room into an entrance hall, adding a service wing and building a stable block from remaining medieval masonry. Several sketches he made of the house survive.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/results?SearchTerms=Hailstone%2c+John%2c+Reverend |title=Anglesey Abbey by the Reverend John Hailstone |website= |publisher=National Trust Collections |access-date=28 February 2020 |quote=}}</ref> He was also responsible for planting trees, including [[Cedrus|cedars]], [[Sequoiadendron giganteum|wellingtonia]], [[weeping elm]] and [[silver lime]], along the drive to the house.<ref name="Guide"/>{{rp|7}} Reverend Hailstone lived in the house after his resignation as vicar of Bottisham in 1861 until he died in 1877. His widow sold it in 1888 to the Reverend James George Clark, who lived there with his family until 1912, when he was given a living in Hertfordshire and tenants were found for Anglesey Abbey.<ref name="Bottisham"/>

[[File:Anglesey Abbey Ad 1926.jpg|right|thumb|upright=1.3|Advertisement for sale of Anglesey Abbey in 1926.]]
Anglesey Abbey was sold in 1926 to two brothers, [[Urban Huttleston Broughton]] (later 1st Baron Fairhaven) and Henry Rogers Broughton, who purchased it for its proximity to the horse-racing town of [[Newmarket, Suffolk|Newmarket]] and their stud at [[Great Barton]] near [[Bury St Edmunds]]. The brothers had inherited a fortune from their maternal grandfather, an American oil baron [[Henry Huttleston Rogers]], and could live a life of leisure devoting themselves to owning and breeding [[Thoroughbred|racehorses]], collecting art and creating gardens. The brothers made several alterations to the house soon after they bought it, converting the monks' day room from an entrance hall into a dining room, moving the front porch, adding a stone newell staircase and putting in fireplaces and panelling. The work was done by architect Sidney Parvin from the London firm of interior designers Turner Lord, and featured in a 1930 edition of [[Country Life (magazine)|'' Country Life'']].<ref name="Treasures">{{cite book | last1 = Purcell | first1 = Mark |last2 = Pearson | first2 = David |last3 = Hale |first3 = William| title = Treasures from Lord Fairhaven's Library at Anglesey Abbey | date = 2013 | publisher = Scala |isbn = 978-1-85759-826-1}}</ref>{{rp|26}}

Henry moved out when he married in 1932, leaving his older brother, by then [[Urban Huttleston Broughton, 1st Baron Fairhaven|Lord Fairhaven]] (having been given the barony that was about to be bestowed on his father, [[Urban H. Broughton]], when he died) as the last private owner of Anglesey Abbey. Lord Fairhaven made extensive additions to the house to provide room for his rapidly expanding collection of books, paintings, tapestries, clocks, furniture and objets d'art. The library wing, designed by Sidney Parvin, was added in 1937 and was followed by the Tapestry Hall, a staircase hall off the dining room, in 1939.<ref name="Treasures"/>{{rp|26}} In 1934 Lord Fairhaven bought and restored Lode Mill on the boundary of his property. The mill had been built in the 18th century but had been converted to grind cement rather than corn in 1900.<ref name="Guide"/>{{rp|27}}

Lord Fairhaven converted the grounds of Anglesey Abbey, which had been largely [[meadow]] and grazing land when the brothers bought the property, into an 18th-century style park with avenues of trees, flower gardens, statuary and ornaments.<ref name="Guide"/>{{rp|24–30}} The final addition to the house, a two-storey picture gallery designed by [[Sir Albert Richardson]], was completed in 1956.<ref name="Treasures"/>{{rp|26}}

When Lord Fairhaven died in 1966, Anglesey Abbey was left to the [[National Trust]] together with an endowment of £300,000.<ref>{{cite news |title=£2 m. Estate of Lord Fairhaven |work=The Times |date=12 September 1966 |page=12}}</ref> Lord Fairhaven had stated in his will that the house should be preserved as "a complete and furnished entity so that it retains as far as possible the character of an English Home".<ref name="Treasures"/>{{rp|11}}

==Interior==
[[File:Fox quern.jpg|right|thumb|200px|A thirteenth century quern in the shape of a sleeping fox in the dining room]]
In addition to its [[Listed building|Grade I listing]], the house is also notable for its contents.<ref name="Treasures"/>{{rp|11}} Lord Fairhaven's collection includes furniture, paintings and sculptures, clocks, tapestries, books, and objets d'art and, according to the author of a guide to Anglesey Abbey, expresses "an eclectic taste and refreshing disregard for fashion".<ref name="Guide"/>{{rp|16}}

Rooms open to the public include the living room that initially formed the chapter house of the monastery and dates from the 13th century; the "oak room" with its oak panelling and plaster ceiling copied from that of the Reindeer Inn at [[Banbury]]; the dining room formed from the monks' day room; the tapestry hall; the service wing; the library, where various royal visitors have engraved their names on a window; several first floor bedrooms; and the two-storey picture gallery.<ref name="Guide"/>

Furniture includes an Italian Renaissance refectory table in the dining room, chairs embroidered by Lord Fairhaven's mother in the living room, a white japanned [[Thomas Chippendale|Chippendale]] dressing table that once belonged to actor [[David Garrick]] in one of the bedrooms, and bookshelves made from the piles of [[John Rennie the Elder|John Rennie's]] [[Waterloo Bridge]] in the library. The tapestry collection includes, as well as seventeenth-century works, one commissioned by Lord Fairhaven from the Cambridge Tapestry Company depicting Anglesey Abbey and the Fairhaven coat-of-arms. There are a large number of clocks in the house with pride of place going to a four-tier pagoda-shaped clock in the living room.<ref name="Guide"/>

The art collection at Anglesey Abbey reflects Lord Fairhaven's taste for British painting of the nineteenth century and earlier, with a particular fondness for views of [[Windsor Castle]], landscapes, animal and bird paintings, and nudes by [[William Etty]]. The twentieth century is represented by paintings by [[Alfred Munnings]], including a picture of a drum horse of the [[1st Life Guards]] (Lord Fairhaven's old regiment), and a portrait by [[Oswald Birley]] of Lord Fairhaven in the ceremonial uniform of his regiment. There are paintings by [[John Constable]], [[Thomas Gainsborough]] (a rare seascape), [[Richard Parkes Bonington]], [[Edwin Landseer]] and [[Abraham Pether|the Pether family]] as well as a series of Tudor portrait panels. Lord Fairhaven collected over 750 paintings, prints and drawings of Windsor Castle. His interest in the castle dates from his youth when his parents had a country house near Windsor, and from when he was later stationed at the castle with his regiment. The Windsor collection was catalogued by art historian Cyril Bunt in 1949.<ref>{{cite book |title=Windsor Castle through three centuries: a description and catalogue of the Windsor collection formed by the Lord Fairhaven |last=Bunt |first=Cyril |publisher=Lewis |location=Leigh-on-Sea |date=1949 |oclc=	64175952}}</ref> Although most of the paintings in Anglesey Abbey are by British artists, foreign artists are represented in the Windsor collection and there are also flower pieces by [[Ambrosius Bosschaert]] and [[Jean-Baptiste Belin|Jean-Baptiste de Fontenay]], as well as three paintings by [[Claude Lorrain]]. Sculpture in the collection includes 18th-century marble horses, a 15th-century continental wooden figure of St Jerome, a bronze bull by [[Antoine-Louis Barye]], and a collection of bronzes by [[R. Tait McKenzie]], [[Frederic Leighton]], [[Alfred Gilbert]] and others, and a silver [[Shield of Achilles]] by [[John Flaxman]].<ref name="Guide"/>

The library at Anglesey Abbey contains over 6,000 books, mostly ordinary reading books in fine bindings with about a thousand collector's books.<ref name="Treasures"/>{{rp|33–4}}

==Grounds==

[[File:Lode mill.14.5.05.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Lode Mill, situated on the edge of the gardens (pictured in May 2005)]]

The 98 acres (400,000 m<sup>2</sup>) of Grade II* listed landscaped grounds at Anglesey Abbey are divided into several avenues, walks, vistas, and gardens, with classical statuary and flowerbeds. It was Lord Fairhaven who laid out the grounds in the style of an eighteenth-century park. He was responsible for replanting the [[rose garden]] and creating the [[dahlia]] garden, the [[Herbaceous border|herbaceous]] garden, the [[Hyacinth (plant)|hyacinth]] garden and the Narcissus garden (so called because it has a statue of [[Narcissus (mythology)|Narcissus]] in it) for seasonal bedding.<ref name="NHLE"/> To commemorate the [[coronation of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth]] in 1937, Lord Fairhaven planted an extensive avenue of trees with a crossing avenue at the far end. The trees used were [[London plane]] alternating with [[horse chestnut]] in four rows, copying those planted in [[Windsor Great Park]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Thomas |first=Graham Stuart |date=2003 |title=Recollections of Great Gardeners |publisher=Frances Lincoln |location=London |page=91}}</ref> Storm damage in 1968 removed most of the plane trees leaving only the horse chestnut trees. The Temple Lawn was created in 1953 to commemorate the [[coronation of Queen Elizabeth II]].<ref name="Guide"/> In front of the house to the south there is a formal lawn and beyond it is a meadow where earthworks mark the position of fishponds from the original priory.<ref name="NHLE"/>

In 1964 American landscape gardener [[Lanning Roper]] wrote a book, ''The Gardens of Anglesey Abbey'', in which he described the careful planning of the garden with its many vistas, avenues, rare and common trees, pools, statues and river temples. He describes how huge areas of sky and mown grass were used to balance symmetrical planting and how Lord Fairhaven used the trees and shrubs to make groups of contrasting colour and foliage.<ref>{{cite book |last=Roper |first=Lanning |date=1964 |title=The Gardens of Anglesey Abbey |publisher=Faber and Faber |location=Cambridgeshire}}</ref> Three generations of the local Ayres family have worked in the gardens since 1921, with Noel and Richard becoming head gardeners.<ref>{{cite book |last=Waterson |first=Merlin |date=1994 |title=The National Trust: the first hundred years |publisher=The National Trust |page=136}}</ref> A Winter Garden was opened in 1998 in Lord Fairhaven's memory.<ref>{{cite book |last=Todd |first=R. |date=2008 |chapter=Planting for winter interest |title=Gardening Secrets from National Trust Head Gardeners |location=London |publisher=National Trust Books |page=41 |isbn=978-1-905400-35-5}}</ref> In 2013 Richard Todd, head gardener at Anglesey Abbey since 1974, received the [[British Empire Medal]] for his years of service to the trust and national heritage.<ref>{{cite news |date=15 June 2013 |title=Queen's Birthday Honours: Straw Bear Festival founder recognised |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-cambridgeshire-22905226 |work=BBC News|access-date= 29 February 2020}}</ref> In 1999 he had been responsible for establishing a composting system to improve drainage and help retain water in a drought. Ten years later 95% of garden waste was composted.<ref>{{cite book |last=Todd |first=R. |date=2008 |chapter=Making Compost |title=Gardening Secrets from National Trust Head Gardeners |location=London |publisher=National Trust Books |page=93 |isbn=978-1-905400-35-5}}.</ref>

[[File:cmglee_Anglesey_Abbey_aerial.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Aerial view of the house and gardens, showing the Summer House at left (June 2013)]]
To the north-west of the house, a block of farm buildings was converted into a large bungalow, complete with a swimming pool, to serve as the Summer House for the Fairhaven family in the days when they used to occupy Anglesey Abbey house in the winter before they moved to [[Kirtling Tower]] in 2004.<ref name="Cam">{{cite news |date=3 March 2017 |title=Available to rent: The Summer House at Anglesey Abbey |url=https://www.cambridgeindependent.co.uk/news/available-to-rent-the-summer-house-at-anglesey-abbey-cambridgeshire-9053588/ |work=Cambridge Independent |access-date= 29 February 2020}}</ref>

The grounds are bounded on the northwest by Bottisham Lode, with Lode Mill, bought and restored by Lord Fairhaven in 1934, at its head. To the south of the mill is the quarry pool, a large pool believed to be the site of a 19th-century [[Coprolite#Coprolite mining|coprolite mine]].<ref name="Guide"/>

==National Trust property==

Anglesey Abbey, officially known as Anglesey Abbey, Gardens and Lode Mill, was until 2020 open to the public all year round. There is an admission charge, with National Trust members having a free entry. In 2025 there were 462,320 visitors to Anglesey Abbey, <ref name=ALVA>{{cite web |title=LATEST VISITOR FIGURES |website=ALVA|url=https://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 |access-date=20 March 2026}}</ref> In 1978 the mill was restored to working order by the Cambridgeshire Wind and Watermill Society and flour can be bought in the mill or the shop. A new visitor centre with a restaurant and shop was opened in 2008. Seasonal attractions include the winter lights festival, [[snowdrop]] and [[Narcissus (plant)|daffodil]] tours in spring, and summer outdoor cinema.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/anglesey-abbey-gardens-and-lode-mill |title=Anglesey Abbey, Gardens and Lode Mill |website=National Trust |access-date=20 March 2023}}</ref>

In March 2020 the property was closed to visitors due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|COVID-19 pandemic]], with the gardens and park re-opening in June 2020.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cambridgeindependent.co.uk/news/parkland-at-cambridgeshires-wimpole-hall-and-anglesey-abbey-to-reopen-9111435/ |title=Parkland at Cambridgeshire's Wimpole Hall and Anglesey Abbey to reopen |website=Cambridge Independent |date=29 May 2020}}</ref>

Anglesey Abbey was featured in the National Trust's 2020 ''Interim Report on the Connections between Colonialism and Properties now in the Care of the National Trust, Including Links with Historic Slavery'' since Samuel Shepheard, who bought the property in 1739 but did not live there or make any additions to it, had been one of the 24 directors of the [[East India Company]] from 1717 to 1721.<ref>
[https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/colionialism-and-historic-slavery-report.pdf Interim Report on the Connections between Colonialism and Properties now in the Care of the National Trust, Including Links with Historic Slavery]</ref>

652500.title: West Wycombe Park
652500.extract:
West Wycombe Park is a country house built between 1740 and 1800 near the village of West Wycombe in Buckinghamshire, England. It was conceived as a pleasure palace for the 18th-century libertine and dilettante Sir Francis Dashwood, 2nd Baronet. The house is a long rectangle with four façades that are columned and pedimented, three theatrically so.  The house encapsulates the entire progression of British 18th-century architecture from early idiosyncratic Palladian to the Neoclassical, although anomalies in its design make it architecturally unique. The mansion is set within an 18th-century landscaped park containing many small temples and follies, which act as satellites to the greater temple, the house.
The house, a Grade I listed building, was given to the National Trust in 1943 by Sir John Dashwood, 10th Baronet (1896–1966), an action strongly resented by his heir. Dashwood retained ownership of the surrounding estate and the contents of the house, most of which he sold; after his death, the house was restored at the expense of his son, the 11th Baronet. Today, while the structure is owned by the National Trust, the house is still the home of the Dashwood family. The house is open to the public during the summer months and is a venue for civil weddings and corporate entertainment, which help to fund its maintenance and upkeep.
